paras: The attempted lynching of George Wilson took place in Birmingham, Alabama, at the end of August 1903, when several white men who had worked with the slain night foreman O. K. Waite twice went to the house of Wilson, a Black former assistant foreman, seeking to kill him. Wilson escaped both times and was then arrested by the police on suspicion of taking part in Waite's killing. The episode is known from a single Birmingham Age-Herald article, which treated it as the prelude to his arrest.

Waite, night foreman of the Birmingham Pipe and Casting company, was shot about midnight on a Tuesday on First avenue near Thirty-second street while walking home, and died the next morning at Hillman hospital. According to the Age-Herald, he was shot by one of a party of four Black men he had passed, one of whom held a grudge against him for a discharge and said, "There is a man I have been looking for to kill for a long time." In the following days the coroner ordered the re-arrest of two of the four, who said they had tried to prevent the shooting, and arrested John Jones, whom they claimed had fired the first shot, while the fourth man was still sought.
Wilson had worked under Waite as assistant night foreman and had been discharged on the Saturday before the killing. It was said that he made threats and "showed considerable feeling in the matter."

Once news of the killing spread, several white men who worked with Waite reportedly became suspicious of Wilson and "made two attempts to kill him." By Wilson's own account, the men came to his house in First alley on Saturday night, and he "barely escaped with his life"; they returned the next night. Each time he sneaked out of the house and crawled "long distances on his hands and feet" to get away. Policeman Ed Jordan was summoned on both nights but found nothing wrong, the men having left before he arrived.

On the night of 1 September, Jordan located Wilson and arrested him on a charge of being implicated in Waite's murder, although his name had not been among those given by the men already under arrest. No arrest of the white men is reported, and the coverage does not show what became of the charge against Wilson. In January 1904 another Black man, Harvey Breeder, was acquitted of Waite's murder and Ed Bryant was released, with no mention of Wilson.

The Birmingham Age-Herald, which followed the Waite case closely, carried the attacks on Wilson on 2 September under the headline "NEGRO MAY BE ONE OF THE ASSASSINS." Its account placed the attempts on Wilson's life in the opening sentence but framed them as the lead-in to his arrest, attributing the motive to the white men's suspicion and offering no comment on their conduct. The details of the attacks came from Wilson himself and from what "it is said," and the white men were not named. No coverage in other white papers or in the Black press was found.

The January 1904 report described Waite as a foreman at Sloss' furnace shot after ordering the accused off the premises, while the August reports placed him at the Birmingham Pipe and Casting works and described a shooting in the street.

bases: Several white co-workers of a slain foreman are said to have twice gone to the house of a Black man suspected in the killing, seeking his life, and he escaped both times (A6).

Wilson was not killed; the papers describe two attempts by 'several white men' acting without authority on suspicion that he took part in Waite's killing, an attempted lynching resting on Wilson's own statement and unattributed report (A6).
The attacks on Wilson's house appear in one Birmingham Age-Herald article, which rests on Wilson's statement and 'it is said' (A6); no other report was found.

accounts.label: Wilson's statement
accounts.gist: Wilson said that twice within three days he had to sneak out of his house and crawl long distances to escape white men seeking his life, on Saturday night and the next night.

accounts.label: Unattributed report ('it is said')
accounts.gist: Several white men who worked with Waite became suspicious of Wilson, who had been discharged and was said to have made threats, and made two attempts to kill him.

accounts.label: Police
accounts.gist: Policeman Jordan, summoned each night, found nothing wrong because the men had left, and later arrested Wilson on suspicion in the murder.

framing.detail: The Age-Herald headlined Wilson as a suspect ('NEGRO MAY BE ONE OF THE ASSASSINS') and reported the attempts on his life without comment or condemnation, as the prelude to his arrest.
